# RescueGPT: An Automated System for Detecting Adverse Safety Events in Prehospital Emergency Medical Service Notes With a Zero‐Shot Approach With Large Language Models: A Proof‐of‐Concept Study

**Authors:** Tina Yi Jin Hsieh; Carl Eriksson; Garth Meckler; Matthew Hansen; Nathan Bahr; Steven Bedrick; Diego Trujillo; Kyu Seo Kim; Byeongyeon Cho; Kai Zhang; Xiaoqian Jiang; Jeanne‐Marie Guise

## Abstract

Traditional adverse safety events (ASE) identification relies on domain experts to manually review and annotate charts, which hinders the scalability of processing high‐volume EMS data. This study explores the use of large language model (LLM) with a knowledge base to automate extraction of adverse safety events (ASE) from unstructured emergency medical service (EMS) notes for pediatric out‐of‐hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) as proof of concept.

Pediatric OHCA records from a national EMS provider were obtained from 2017 to 2020. Leveraging the Pediatric Prehospital Adverse Safety Event Detection System (PEDS) as a foundational knowledge base, we used the LinkML framework to develop an ontology to define ASEs across six essential EMS care domains. To convert unstructured EMS narratives into structured prompts, we used the Structured Prompt Interrogation and Recursive Extraction of Semantics (SPIRES) method, which generated schema‐driven prompts to guide the GPT‐3.5 model in identifying ASEs. By mapping unstructured data into structured concepts consistent with PEDS guidelines, the model produced targeted prompts that supported effective entity extraction.

We evaluated framework effectiveness with accuracy, recall, precision, F1 score, and specificity across 42 pediatric OHCA cases covering ASE‐related entities. RescueGPT showed high accuracy in detecting common ASEs (Patient Rhythm, Age, Weight, Length) but revealed challenges in rare events (Failure to Establish IV Access, Incorrect Airway Equipment Size, Failure to Ventilate Patient) likely due to more inconsistent and complex documentation.

RescueGPT demonstrates potential in scaling automated ASE detection, but performance varies by completeness and clarity of EMS narrative, particularly with rare events. Fragmented clinical documentation limits accuracy and highlights the need for standardized collection protocols in EMS systems. Future directions will focus on implementing rebalancing strategies for rare events, applying explainability methods to improve decision‐making transparency, and refining text segmentation techniques to handle mixed outcomes to further improve performance.

## Introduction

Pediatric out‐of‐hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is an important contributor to child mortality and contributes to the loss of disability‐adjusted life years (DALYs) within the US [1]. While there have been marked improvements in survival rates from in‐hospital pediatric cardiac arrests and adult OHCAs over the past 10–15 years, survival rates for pediatric OHCA remain relatively stagnant [2]. EMS plays a critical role in the healthcare system's response to medical emergencies such as OHCAs, as timely and effective early interventions may significantly enhance the chance of survival. Our prior research in prehospital care for pediatric OHCA has identified potential mild or severe adverse safety events (ASE) related to resuscitation in up to 60% of cases [3].

Children affected by OHCA emergencies are especially prone to ASEs, which span from healthcare‐associated deaths to injuries and other complications [4, 5]. The conventional gold standard for identifying ASEs involves time‐intensive manual reviews of medical charts by highly trained physicians, a process which, even assuming short charts (1–3 pages) and highly experienced physician reviewers, requires roughly seven to 10 min per EMS chart [4, 6]. Expert manual medical chart review is not only time‐intensive but expensive. An automated approach to detect ASEs has the potential to improve the efficiency of patient safety and quality reviews in EMS, enabling rapid identification of statewide, regional, and agency‐specific opportunities to improve care and identify areas for additional training.

Developing conventional machine learning models necessitates extensive and expensive chart review and annotation by domain experts increasing cost and limiting the feasibility of developing these models. State‐of‐the‐art large language models (LLMs) create promising new avenues for analyzing unstructured free‐text data. Foundation models like GPT‐3 [7] and GPT‐4 [8] from OpenAI, which do not require task‐specific training, have been successfully applied in clinical settings to extract structured information from medical reports and synthesize evidence with limited data [9]. These models, while innovative, come with challenges such as difficulties in generalizing, issues with understanding negations [10], and a tendency to produce incorrect information, known as hallucinations [11]. To overcome these challenges, integrating LLMs with structured knowledge bases (KBs) and ontologies has been a focus of recent research [12, 13]. These frameworks store and organize domain‐specific information, enabling logical reasoning and factual validation.

Integrating the adaptability of LLMs with the precision of KBs and ontologies has led to advanced methodologies that combine entity extraction with relationship understanding, promoting a more comprehensive text analysis compared to traditional named entity recognition methods [13]. Utilizing ontologies helps validate data before incorporating it into KBs, addressing LLM limitations and enhancing adaptability of the model.

## Research Focus

The objective of the proof‐of‐concept study is to develop a streamlined tool “RescueGPT,” where RESCUE stands for Recognition, Extraction, Surveillance, and Conceptualization Using EMS notes, which leverages LLMs and incorporates domain‐specific knowledge bases from clinical pediatric and emergency medicine experts for the efficient named entity recognition (NER), extraction, and conceptualization of EMS charts, targeting the identification and tracking of preventable ASEs in pediatric OHCA cases.

## Methods

### ASE Identification Process

We utilized the Pediatric Prehospital Adverse Safety Event Detection System (PEDS) tool [6, 14] to identify ASEs that constitute our knowledge base. The PEDS tool is a rule‐based system that incorporates expert knowledge from a clinical panel to detect ASEs in six key domains of care: (1) Assessment and diagnosis, (2) Clinical decision‐making, (3) Procedures, (4) Airway, (5) Medications, and (6) Fluids. The PEDS tool was previously developed by our team and validated in prior studies [3, 4, 5, 6]. We used a similar process as in previous studies to review medical records including using physicians board‐certified in pediatric emergency or critical care medicine, rigorous chart review training, and dual review for all charts with resolution of disagreements by consensus. EMS clinical notes were collected in partnership with a large nationwide provider of EMS transport for children < 18 years with OHCA from 2017 to 2020. The study was approved by Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center's Institutional Review Board as exempt.

### Ontology Development

To transform unstructured clinical text data into structured, meaningful concepts pertinent to pediatric OHCA, we employed the LinkML framework [15] to construct our ontology schema, informed by the PEDS tool [6, 14]. This structure lays the groundwork for systematically organizing and understanding the data (Figure 1).

### Prompt Generation

Next, leveraging a two‐part input system, we applied the Structured Prompt Interrogation and Recursive Extraction of Semantics (SPIRES) method [12]. This involves the integration of the LinkML‐generated schema, derived from the PEDS tool, with the unstructured text from EMS notes. This process facilitates the generation of targeted prompts for the GPT‐3.5 model, a transformer‐based autoregressive language model with 175 million parameters [7], ensuring the extraction of structured information while maintaining HIPAA compliance via Azure AI. The extracted data, formatted according to the predefined LinkML schema, undergoes a validation process to ensure its alignment with the corresponding concepts within the ontology. This results in a structured representation of domain‐specific knowledge, enabling researchers and healthcare professionals to query and analyze the information effectively. The complex relations between named entities captured by the KB‐informed model enhance accuracy compared to conventional named entity recognition methods.

### ASE Analysis

We then selected a sample of 42 EMS notes to analyze using RescueGPT, focusing on its capability to accurately identify and classify nine specific entities: Patient age, rhythm, weight/length, “Failure To Successfully Establish IV(Intravenous) or IO (intraosseous) Access,” “IV IO Placement Delay In Access,” “Multiple Vascular Access Attempts IV or IO,” “Failure To Ventilate Patient,” “Intubation Too Many Attempts,” and “Incorrect Airway Equipment Size Tube Size Half Size Off.” We assessed RescueGPT's performance using accuracy, recall, precision, F1 score, and specificity metrics. ### Good Accuracy Across Entities With Identified Areas for Improvement

The performance of RescueGPT, with accuracy scores ranging from 0.74 to 0.98, showcases overall effectiveness, especially in relatively straightforward entities like “Patient Rhythm” (accuracy: 0.98) and “Patient Age” (accuracy: 0.95). However, “Failure to Successfully Establish IV or IO Access” exhibits a lower accuracy (0.74) and the highest rate of false positives (9 out of 42, Figure 2), highlighting an area for improvement. This challenge is evident when failure and success appear in the same sentence, leading to misclassifications by RescueGPT. Examples include scenarios such as “IO UNSUCCESSFUL IN R TIBIA, IV STARTED R AC 20GA. EPI GIVEN X3 AS CHARTED” and “A PEDIATRIC IO WAS ATTEMPTED IN UPPER LEFT ARM BUT WAS NOT APPROPRIATE SIZE FOR THE PT. ANOTHER IO ATTEMPT WAS MADE LEFT FEMUR AND WAS SUCCESSFUL”(Table 4), where the model incorrectly interprets the ultimate outcome as a failure. This indicates that RescueGPT struggles with contextual understanding in complex medical narratives where multiple outcomes are described in the same sentence. Enhancing RescueGPT's ability to interpret nuanced language and sequential medical procedures could reduce these false positives, improving its performance and reliability in emergency care settings.

### Optimal Specificity but Poor Precision, Recall, and F1 Scores for Two Entities (Rare Events)

Two entities, “Incorrect Airway Equipment Size Tube Size Half Size Off” and “Failure to Ventilate Patient” exhibit poor precision, recall, and F1 scores metrics due to the low incidence of positive events in the dataset. For “Incorrect Airway Equipment Size,” only 5 out of 42 cases are positive, and for “Failure to Ventilate Patient,” there are only 4 positive cases (ASE present) (Figure 2), both outnumbered by the negative events (ASE not present), leading to high specificity but poor precision and recall (Figure 3). While the model efficiently identifies normal situations, it fails to accurately detect these rare yet critical events. Improving these metrics may involve dataset rebalancing, applying cost‐sensitive learning, or using anomaly detection techniques to enhance training on these essential but infrequent cases.

## Discussion and Conclusions

Adverse safety events and errors that occur during the delivery of care are one of the leading causes of preventable death and morbidity. Being able to identify and characterize ASEs at scale would be a major step forward in the pathway to prevention.

Large language models are increasingly applied to automate extraction and unlock insights from unstructured or free‐text clinical narratives, with techniques like prompt engineering, zero‐shot [16, 17, 18], few‐shot [19], chain‐of‐thought [20, 21], instruction‐based named entity recognition (NER) [22], fine‐tuning [23, 24], retrieval‐augmented generation (e.g., knowledge graph‐enhanced RAG [25]), semantic similarity filtering [26], or hybrid frameworks [27, 28], among others. The SPIRES method [12] goes beyond methods that focus on classification, summarization, or NER, enabling structured knowledge‐based summary assembly though schema‐guided recursion, zero‐shot prompting and ontology grounding, without the need of fine‐tuning or retrieval systems.

To our knowledge, RescueGPT is the first tool to explore the application of the schema‐driven prompting approach (SPIRES) combined with a pediatric emergency medicine ontology to leverage expert domain‐specific knowledge in identifying pediatric ASEs through zero‐shot learning. This study represents an important step in combining LLMs with ontologies developed by experts to assist in improving emergency care by identifying opportunities for improvement in care rapidly and at low cost.

RescueGPT's performance is influenced by the quality and completeness of the ontologies it ingests, as well as the complexity of the narratives. The algorithm's ability to accurately parse and understand these narratives is critical yet currently hampered by existing data quality and structure issues. OHCA care follows a more well‐established care algorithm than many other medical conditions, suggesting that developing ontologies and establishing the gold standard for ASEs in other clinical scenarios could be more challenging. A particular challenge arises with identifying rare events, such as “Failure To Successfully Establish IV or IO Access.” These instances often result in lower F1 scores due to the model's difficulty maintaining high precision and recall amidst the dominance of negative and nonapplicable cases. RescueGPT's accuracy also suffers when clinical narratives combine successes and failures in a single sentence. To address this, we plan to improve its ability to parse complex sentences by segmenting the text and using these segments to generate a series of focused prompts based on partial schemas. This approach should enable RescueGPT to understand the sequence of events better and avoid misclassifications.

There are also notable gaps in specific clinical information within EMS notes. For instance, many notes lack critical details like tube size (required for assessment of “Incorrect Airway Equipment Size Tube Size Half Size Off”) or exact timestamps for procedures (Ex, assessing “Failure To Ventilate Patient” requires information on time), which are crucial for accurate medical assessment. This lack of specific information points to a broader issue within data collection protocols in EMS, suggesting a need for standardized, detailed clinical documentation because “the model is only as good as the data it is trained on.”

To ensure RescueGPT works effectively across different regions and patient populations, we need to validate its generalizability. Currently, the model is trained on data from a specific group of highly experienced pediatric and emergency physicians. We plan to conduct broader validation studies using real‐world EMS records from the National EMS Information System (NEMSIS) across various states. This will help us assess how well RescueGPT performs on data from different emergency care practices and diverse patient populations.

Moreover, the absence of a “Non‐Applicable” category within the model's schema has led to interpretative challenges, notably when information is missing from EMS narratives. Introducing this category could significantly improve RescueGPT's interpretive accuracy by allowing it to classify cases where specific details are not mentioned appropriately.

In addition, developing explainability methods is essential for building trust in RescueGPT's reasoning. Similar to how attention maps [29] visualize focus points in computer vision models, explainability methods in healthcare can reveal RescueGPT's decision‐making logic. This transparency is vital because, unlike other domains, potential biases or errors in RescueGPT could have severe consequences. By understanding the model's rationale, healthcare professionals can assess its trustworthiness in specific cases [30], ultimately leading to more informed patient care decisions. Explainability methods can also pinpoint areas where the model struggles, guiding further development and refinement.

Last but not least, it is important to ensure the dynamic nature of domain knowledge to ensure RescueGPT's effectiveness. Medical best practices constantly evolve, necessitating a model that adapts. To address this, we envision continuous updates through regular ontology refreshes to reflect advancing medical knowledge, active learning with human feedback for real‐world scenario refinement, and potential integration with real‐time data sources containing latest clinical guidelines [31]. Such a dynamic approach will ensure RescueGPT remains a valuable tool for pediatric OHCA analysis and contributes to improved patient outcomes in the ever‐changing healthcare landscape.

## Conclusions

RescueGPT shows promise for automating the analysis of pediatric OHCA cases and it requires further refinement of its knowledge base, data collection methods, and handling of complex narratives. With these refinements, RescueGPT can be a valuable tool for efficient, accurate, and scalable identification of ASEs occurring during the care of pediatric OHCA. This integration of LLMs with structured knowledge bases unlocks vast potential in analyzing unstructured data like EMS narratives, paving the way for advancements in ASE detection and ultimately leading to better decision‐making. In the future, tools such as RescueGPT may be deployed by individual EMS agencies to reduce the burden of quality assurance work, deployed by a state or region to conduct large scale evaluations of emergency care quality, and/or with further refinements, may become embedded in electronic medical records as early warning systems.

# Randomized controlled trial of traxi panniculus retractor use during non‐emergent cesarean delivery

**Authors:** Tooba Anwer; Tina Yi Jin Hsieh; Emily Stonestreet; Audrey Mutoni; Phillip Hess; Yunping Li; Tyler Lueck; Michael Furdyna; John Kowalczyk; Anna Modest; Ai‐ris Y Collier

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2 Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3 Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4 Department of Anesthesiology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 5 Department of Anesthesiology, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

The objective of our study is to determine whether the use of a self‐retaining panniculus retraction device (traxi) in patients with obesity will improve operative time, pulmonary function, or patient and provider experience for non‐emergent cesarean delivery.

Pregnant patients with body mass index (BMI) ≥40 kg/m2 undergoing non‐emergent cesarean delivery were recruited from two academic hospitals and randomized to traxi panniculus retraction or to no traxi. Computer‐generated block randomization, stratified by prior abdominal surgery, was used to randomize participants in a 1:1 ratio to the traxi or standard care. Demographic information was collected by self‐report. Surgical time from skin incision to closure and clinical data was collected by review of the electronic health record. Pulmonary function testing via spirometer was performed before and after application of retraction. Participant and provider experience was collected postoperatively. Intention‐to‐treat analysis was performed using a Wilcoxon rank‐sum test and a chi‐squared test for continuous and dichotomous variables, respectively.

We enrolled 135 participants from 2018 to 2024 at two academic hospitals; 67 were randomized to traxi and 68 were randomized to no traxi. Of these, 43 (31.9%) reported no prior abdominal surgery (including prior cesarean or other laparotomy) and the median BMI was 48.9 (interquartile range [IQR] 45.0, 52.5). The trial was terminated before the target sample size of 220 participants was achieved due to slow accrual and waning clinical equipoise. Baseline characteristics of each group were similar. Median surgical time was 65.0 min (IQR 55.0, 81.0) in the traxi group and 70.0 min (IQR 57.0, 86.0) in the no traxi group, but this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.31). There was less restrictive pulmonary physiology associated with application of traxi compared to no traxi; the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) difference was −0.03 L (−0.20, 0.10) and −0.11 L (−0.45, −0.02) (p = 0.048), respectively. Providers were significantly more likely to report that the traxi was very effective, not really difficult to use, not really physically uncomfortable to use, very satisfying to use, and a form of retraction that they would very likely recommend to another colleague. All patients in the traxi arm reported they would choose this retraction method in a future cesarean delivery compared to 91% of patients in the no traxi arm; however, this finding was not statistically significant (p = 0.05). “A little bit” of rash where the method of taping was used within 2 days of surgery was reported by 0% of patients in the traxi arm, compared to the no traxi arm (20%, p = 0.0048).

Traxi panniculus retraction did not significantly improve surgical time but was associated with less restrictive pulmonary function testing compared with the control arm; these findings should be interpreted in the context of the study's limited sample size. There were higher reports of provider satisfaction with use of traxi compared to the control arm. Patient‐reported satisfaction with use of traxi was high but not statistically different when compared to the control arm with the exception of patient‐reported rash (less in traxi arm).

Keywords: cesarean delivery, obesity, panniculus retraction, surgical time

## INTRODUCTION

The prevalence of maternal obesity in the United States has increased steadily in recent decades. According to the 2019 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 29% of pregnant individuals have prepregnancy obesity, up from 26.1% in 2017 [1]. The World Health Organization defines obesity as a body mass index (BMI) greater than or equal to 30.0 kg/m2 and class III obesity as a BMI exceeding 40 kg/m2 [2, 3]. Additionally, class III obesity correlates with a 2.89 increased odds of cesarean delivery [4], and a 3.76 increased odds for fetal distress [5], compared to normal weight individuals. With increasing BMI, the rate of achieving complete dilation decreases. Patients with class III obesity can experience prolonged labor and failure to progress, indicating the need for a cesarean delivery [6]. Postoperatively, patients with increased BMI are at a higher risk for postpartum hemorrhage and wound complications [7, 8].

Some patients with class III or greater obesity have an overhanging abdominal panniculus that can create a challenge during cesarean delivery through obstruction of the surgical field or difficulty with delivering the fetus. With a low transverse skin incision, panniculus retraction may be necessary to achieve adequate surgical field visualization. Typical panniculus retraction methods include elevating the panniculus onto the maternal chest wall using medical tape or manual retraction cephalad with the help of additional personnel. Pulmonary function testing can be used to determine if patients experience a restrictive breathing pattern (reduced forced vital capacity volume or the total amount of air one can forcefully exhale in a single breath after taking the deepest breath possible). A reduction in forced vital capacity occurs likely from two mechanisms: first from external chest wall compression as the panniculus displacement superiorly limits expansion of the rib cage and chest wall during inspiration and second from a cephalad force applied to the diaphragm from upward retraction of the panniculus and upward pressure of abdominal contents. Although commercial retraction devices are available, there is limited published data on their efficacy.

The traxi panniculus retractor was designed to reliably retract the panniculus during surgery, thereby reducing the need for extra personnel for retraction, improving visualization to decrease operating time, and improving patient satisfaction with the delivery experience by preserving patient dignity [9]. Of note, it is intentionally spelled with lowercase letters by its manufacturer Laborie. Despite these claims and the FDA class I exemption on the device, there is little evidence to support its use during cesarean delivery. The primary objective of our study is to determine whether use of the traxi device for panniculus retraction during non‐emergent cesarean delivery compared to no traxi is associated with improved operating times. Our secondary objectives were to quantify the differences in pulmonary function, postsurgical events, neonatal outcomes, and patient and provider‐reported satisfaction when traxi was utilized for panniculus retraction in non‐emergent cesarean deliveries in patients with class III obesity.

## METHODS

### Study population

We conducted this open‐label, randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate the use of traxi for patients with class III obesity undergoing non‐emergent cesarean delivery at two tertiary care centers. Before initiation of the study, Institutional Review Board approval was obtained at both sites. The clinical trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov. Participants were screened and assessed for eligibility by trained study staff who reviewed the labor and delivery operating schedule, antepartum census, and obstetrical clinic schedule in advance. Participants were then recruited and enrolled by trained study staff once cesarean delivery was confirmed to be the planned method of delivery. Participants were included if they were at least 18 years old, had a BMI greater than or equal to 40 kg/m2 at the time of delivery, had a retractable panniculus, were undergoing non‐emergent cesarean delivery, had a singleton live gestation, and were able to provide written, informed consent. A panniculus was determined to be retractable by the physician if it obstructed the location of Pfannenstiel incision when the patient was lying in the dorsal supine position. Patients were excluded if they had a disruption of abdominal skin such as infection, rash, abrasion, or laceration, or had a known adhesive allergy. Baseline demographic and obstetrical history were obtained through self‐report and through review of the electronic medical record.

### Randomization

Participants who met eligibility criteria and provided written informed consent were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the traxi arm or no traxi (control) arm using a computer‐generated block randomization. Randomization was stratified by either a history of prior cesarean delivery or open abdominal surgery.

### Pulmonary function tests

The pulmonary effects of panniculus retraction were investigated using pulmonary function tests (PFTs) employing a handheld portable spirometry device. This approach was deemed convenient due to the straightforward training required for device operation, its compact design suitable for use in the labor and delivery operating room (L&D OR), and its general familiarity among our anesthesia colleagues. The bedside portable spirometry was not performed to formally diagnose restrictive and obstructive pulmonary disease as traditional PFT testing is intended to do. The portable spirometry for this study was only utilized to assess for change in participant PFT parameters pre‐ and post‐retraction. Participants were not excluded based on preoperative PFT results, nor were they excluded from analysis if PFT was unable to be performed as a secondary outcome of the protocol. When trained study team members were available to perform the PFTs, a portable spirometry device (EasyOne Air, NDD 2500‐2A, FlowTube NDD 5050‐50) was used to measure the forced vital capacity (FVC) in liters (L), forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) in L, and the ratio of FEV1/FVC. FVC is the total volume of air exhaled during a maximal forced breath. FEV1 measures the volume of air exhaled in the first second of this forced breath. The FEV1/FVC ratio is the proportion of the total FVC that can be exhaled in the first second and is used to distinguish between obstructive and restrictive lung disease. These parameters were collected to determine if the method of panniculus retraction affects pulmonary function during cesarean delivery. The participants were first instructed on spirometry in the preoperative space. Patients were asked to take a deep breath and blow into the spirometer tube with maximum effort. These trials were repeated until the device indicated “good effort” with three practice trials. In the operating room, prior to surgery start, measurements were recorded while the participant was in the supine position (with a wedge in place). The pre‐retraction PFTs were performed while the patient was lying supine on the operating table with the wedge in place. The post‐retraction method PFTs were performed after the retraction method was placed while the patient was still in the operating room in the supine position and prior to the start of the cesarean delivery. Three trials of PFTs were performed pre‐ and post‐retraction, with the best effort recorded. The participant was in the same (supine) position for the pre‐ and post‐retraction PFTs. Individual participant differences (pre‐retraction minus post‐retraction) in FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC were calculated as a secondary outcome. A difference in PFTs in the negative direction indicates an increase in restrictive physiology following application of the panniculus retraction method.

### Surgical retraction

For those randomized to traxi, the sterile, single‐use retraction device was applied. The application of the device is straightforward and stepwise, following the tabs labeled A through C per manufacturer guidelines [10]. Clinicians applying the device underwent formal training by industry representatives or through video instructions provided by the manufacturer in the application of the device. After the device was applied, the abdominal skin preparation was performed over the incision site and the traxi device as usual. The traxi was supplied by the company Laborie for the use of the study, and the device was not charged to the participant's account. Those randomized to the no traxi arm were asked to use standard of care methods of retraction (other than traxi) at the discretion of the surgeons performing the cesarean (extra personnel, taping with medical tape, additional self‐retaining retractors such as the Alexis O retractor, etc.). The retraction methods were removed at the conclusion of the procedure.

### Obstetric, surgical, and neonatal outcomes

The primary outcome measure was duration of cesarean delivery (in minutes) from skin incision to skin closure. The times are documented in the labor and delivery encounter recorded by the nursing staff in the electronic medical record. All secondary outcomes were collected by review of the operative report and medical record. Secondary outcome measures included time from incision to delivery (minutes), estimated blood loss (mL), need for intraoperative or postpartum transfusion, number of scrubbed personnel, level of training of first assistant, readmission, wound infections, chorioamnionitis, and change in spirometry post‐retraction. Neonatal outcomes including birthweight, 1‐ and 5‐minute Apgar scores, neonatal intensive care unit admission, and infant sex at birth were collected. Neonatal cord gases were not collected.

### Provider‐ and patient‐reported outcomes

After completion of surgery, we assessed provider satisfaction by administering a brief questionnaire developed by our research team. The survey was distributed to personnel involved in the delivery (including obstetricians, anesthesiologists, residents, fellows, physician assistants, surgical technicians, students, and nursing staff) on paper or via Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap 14.5.43) database. Paper surveys were administered to participants during their postpartum stay and collected prior to discharge. Electronic surveys were sent via REDCap to patient emails after delivery occurred if patient had not answered the survey prior to hospital discharge. Participant satisfaction was also assessed using a questionnaire (Suppl. Methods) developed by our research team made available on paper or via REDCap 14.5.43 [11].

### Sample size calculation

Our sample size calculation is based on data from a prior study that reported total operative time (incision to closure) by BMI [12]. In that study, for patients with a BMI ≥40 kg/m2, the median total operative time was 55.0 min (± 26 min). Using a two‐sided alpha of 0.05, in order to achieve 85% power to detect a difference of 10 min and allowing for 15% loss to follow‐up, we aimed to enroll 120 participants per arm.

### Statistical analysis

Traxi and no traxi groups were analyzed using an intention‐to‐treat (ITT) approach. Continuous variables were assessed for normality and presented as median and interquartile range (IQR). Wilcoxon rank sum tests were used to compare groups. Categorical variables were compared with chi‐squared tests and presented as column percentages. For participant and provider responses, multi‐choice variables were dichotomized based on clinical relevance. Nonnormally distributed data were analyzed with nonparametric tests. Multiple provider respondents per participant's delivery were recorded, and providers could respond for multiple participants. Although some providers had multiple participants enrolled in the study, the provider was given a survey for each participant because each encounter was considered clinically meaningful given different patient and surgical characteristics, which contributed to the heterogeneity of experiences. Responses from providers were analyzed by group based on the total number of surveys received rather than on a per‐patient basis. The post‐intervention minus pre‐intervention differences in PFT metrics (FEV1 difference, FVC difference, and FEV1/FVC difference) between groups were calculated with 95% confidence interval. For all analyses, a two‐sided significance level of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc.).

## RESULTS

We approached 243 participants and enrolled 142 participants from December 2018 to August 2024, resulting in 135 participants who completed the study—68 in the traxi group and 67 in the no traxi group (Figure 1). One participant who needed general anesthesia was excluded for multiple reasons: general anesthesia prompts surgeons to perform a “faster” cesarean delivery to minimize anesthetic risks to the neonate, the participant would not be able to complete the satisfaction survey given they were asleep during the procedure, and intubation precludes the performance of bedside PFTs. Due to slow accrual rates (more providers desiring to use traxi instead of participating in study and possibly being randomized to no traxi), the study team elected to halt the study prior to completing planned enrollment given that enrollment, at the current rate, may require several more years and be more hindered by waning clinical equipoise (strong preference by providers to use traxi). Additionally, an interim analysis had not been planned in the study design. Six enrolled participants were found ineligible after randomization, and 1 was administratively withdrawn. The median BMI was 48.9 m/kg2 (IQR: 45.0–52.5) and 92 (68%) had a history of prior open abdominal surgery. The baseline characteristics for traxi and no traxi groups were similar in terms of age, demographics, obstetrical history, and surgical indications (Table 1).

Regarding PFT data, spirometry enables the detection of restriction of pulmonary volumes related to chest wall compression from panniculus retraction. Restrictive pathology is expected to demonstrate a reduction in FEV1 and FVC with a normal or elevated FEV1/FVC. The FEV1 difference was −0.03 L (−0.20, 0.10) in the traxi arm and −0.11 L (−0.45, −0.02) in the no traxi arm, indicating less restrictive pulmonary physiology after traxi placement than no traxi, p = 0.048. There were no significant differences in FVC or FEV1/FVC ratio pre and post use of the retraction method between the control and the traxi arm (Table 2). PFT data were available for 71 (50%) of the participants and these participants had similar characteristics to the overall cohort with the exception of a greater proportion of participants in the no PFT group having cesarean for category II fetal heart rate tracing (Table S1).

In post‐delivery provider surveys, there were 219 provider responses completed in the traxi group and 169 responses in the no traxi arm. The majority (74%) of providers reported that the traxi device was a very effective method for panniculus retraction compared to 38% in the no traxi group (p < 0.0001). Additionally, 40% of providers in the no traxi group perceived the method to be difficult to use, whereas 23% of providers in the traxi group found that the traxi was difficult to use (p = 0.0003). Eighty‐three percent of providers utilizing traxi indicated that it was either “not really” or “not at all” physically uncomfortable to use, in contrast to 49% of the no traxi group (p < 0.0001). Providers using no traxi were less likely to perceive that the patient was comfortable (20%) compared to the traxi group (12%, p = 0.028). Providers in the traxi group reported very high satisfaction with the retraction method (70%) compared to the no traxi group (30%, p < 0.0001) and were more likely to recommend traxi use to colleagues (71%) compared to the no traxi method (27%, p < 0.0001; Table 4). The comments from providers who answered “somewhat,” “ undecided,” “ not really,” or “not at all” to whether they would recommend the device included the following: “patient felt to be very tight, not sure if this is due to the traxi device retracting the pannus,” “method was helpful but time consuming to apply, as the nurses applying it were not familiar with the instructions…more use of the device and familiarity with it will result in improved speed of application,” “it got wet with prepping and became less effective,” and “team was not sure how to use and took some time calling around for suggested use.”

## DISCUSSION

In this RCT that focused on pregnant individuals with class III obesity undergoing non‐emergent cesarean delivery, the utilization of the traxi did not lead to a statistically significant reduction in overall operating time. However, secondary outcomes (which the study was not powered for) showed that application of the traxi, compared to no traxi, resulted in less restrictive pulmonary physiology. Generally, participants tended to be satisfied with either retraction method. There were higher satisfaction levels for providers when the traxi was used for panniculus retraction. Patients reported less rash after traxi application; however, none of the other metrics of satisfaction were significantly different between treatment arms. Importantly, there were no differences in maternal or neonatal morbidity rates between the group that received the traxi and the no traxi group. It is well established that obesity increases the risk of cesarean delivery via a host of mechanisms, including pre‐existing comorbidities and obstetric complications, slower progression of labor, and a prolongation of pregnancy past the estimated due date [13]. Previous studies have evaluated methods of improving operative outcomes in women with obesity undergoing cesarean delivery. A study of the self‐retaining symmetrical Mobius retractor found no improvement in post‐cesarean delivery discomfort or operative times [14]. A study of patient survey responses post‐cesarean delivery found that the use of a panniculus retraction device applied after cesarean delivery did not significantly reduce total opioid use after cesarean delivery [15]. One RCT of 150 participants evaluated the use of traxi to retract the panniculus during fetal ultrasound and found that while its use was well tolerated by patients and ultrasonographers, it did not improve the ability to obtain complete fetal anatomic views [16]. However, we did not encounter any studies investigating operative outcomes with the use of traxi during cesarean delivery. While our study did not have statistical power to demonstrate whether traxi reduces operative time or surgical risks during cesarean delivery, secondary outcomes demonstrated that providers who used the traxi had rated higher satisfaction scores compared to providers who used control retraction methods. Patients randomized to traxi were more likely to recommend traxi retraction compared to those in the control method of retraction.

Notably, PFTs demonstrated that use of the traxi did not lead to a more restrictive respiratory physiology. Obesity is independently associated with impaired maternal respiratory function during cesarean delivery, and patients with obesity tend to experience greater reductions in spirometric parameters after neuraxial anesthesia; however, there is no evidence available to date that evaluates whether panniculus retraction further exacerbates pulmonary restriction beyond the effects of obesity and anesthesia [17]. During panniculus retraction during cesarean delivery, there is concern that superior displacement of the panniculus may shift pressure to the thoracic cavity and create restrictive pulmonary physiology. Our results demonstrated that the FEV1 difference (post application FEV1 − pre application FEV1) was −0.03 L (−0.20, 0.10) in the traxi arm and −0.11 L (−0.45, −0.02) in the no traxi arm, p = 0.048. This suggests that while the FEV1 decreased post application of both traxi and retraction in the control arm, that the decrease in FEV1 was to a lesser extent in the traxi arm compared to control, indicating a less restrictive and more protective pulmonary physiology compared to the control. These findings may be attributed to the more equalized distribution of the panniculus across the thoraco‐abdominal cavity using the traxi compared to the control arm.

The study's strengths include that it is a prospective randomized trial design, which can enhance the validity of the findings by minimizing bias and confounding factors. Additionally, the enrollment of patients from two tertiary care centers increases the generalizability and applicability of the results, acknowledging the variability in operating practices across different institutions. Furthermore, the study's inclusion of both nulliparous and multiparous patients, stratified by history of previous abdominal surgery, allows for a comprehensive assessment of the intervention's effects across diverse patient populations. Moreover, the incorporation of survey‐based subjective data from both providers and participants offers valuable insights into the often‐neglected but crucial aspect of patient and provider experience. These qualitative data complement the objective outcomes and contribute to a more holistic understanding of the intervention's impact. While the traxi was supplied by the manufacturer for the study, the list price per one traxi retractor is $75.25 compared to the list price per one Alexis O retractor, which is $93.00. These details may be useful when balancing price per product and cost per minute in the operating room, which was estimated to be $36–37 per minute using financial data from California's short‐term general and specialty hospitals in FY2014 [18].

The trial is limited by its premature conclusion due to challenges encountered in the recruitment process and diminishing equipoise. The originally planned sample size was calculated based on a study that demonstrated a median total operative time of 55.0 minutes for patients with a BMI greater than or equal to 40 km/m2. However, the actual median operating time in our standard of care arm was 65 minutes. The original target sample size of 240 was not achieved due to a lower‐than‐expected number of eligible patients and a shift in the standard of care during the study period as the traxi device became more frequently requested. While the providers’ preference for traxi use may have been reflected in the provider survey responses, the availability of the device for use outside of the study was unlikely to play a large bias in the provider responses as the main site 1 hospital (88% of enrollment) did not have the traxi available for use outside of this research protocol. However, increased provider experience and familiarity with the traxi device led to reluctance to have patients randomized to the no traxi group, reducing power and potentially contributing to the non‐significant primary and secondary outcomes. This shift toward routine traxi use effectively eliminated the clinical equipoise—the state of genuine uncertainty about the comparative merits of the intervention—that is essential for conducting a scientifically rigorous randomized trial. While the data showed no evidence of traxi being unsafe (maternal infection, hemorrhage, or NICU admission), the study's size was insufficient to detect infrequent but potentially significant adverse events. Additionally, PFT data were not available for all of the enrolled participants given there was not always a provider trained in PFT collection available during all enrollment hours. Blinding participants and personnel to the retraction method was not technically feasible.

In conclusion, traxi panniculus retraction did not significantly improve surgical time but was associated with less restrictive pulmonary function parameters compared to the control arm. Providers in the traxi arm reported significantly higher satisfaction scores post procedure compared to those who were in the control arm. Patient‐reported outcomes were similar in both arms with only significantly reduced rates of self‐reported rash in the 2 days following surgery in the traxi arm.

Abstract 41

Background 42

Clinical data analysis typically requires statistical programming skills, whereas 43

cloud-based artificial intelligence (AI) agents risk exposing sensitive patient records. 44

We developed and functionally validated a privacy-preserving, zero-code 45

conversational statistical analysis framework that translates natural-language clinical 46

research requests into executable R workflows while strictly retaining raw patient data 47

within local computing environments. 48

Methods 49

Orchestrated by the n8n engine, the system integrates the DeepSeek-Reasoner model 50

equivalently translated into efficient research output. Despite increasing data 133

Construction of the Clinical Research and Biostatistics Knowledge Base 324

The Pinecone vector database stores five categories of domain knowledge: R 325

programming standards, publication-style figure templates, biostatistical methodology 326

guidance, R package recommendations, and interactive requirement templates. During 327

models in medical statistical tasks at two levels. First, the verified statistical strategies 332

This step reduces the likelihood of unsupported assumptions when analytical 340

information is incomplete. Although RAG cannot eliminate all coding or 341

Discussion 415

In this proof-of-concept study, we developed and functionally validated a 416

human-supervised, zero-code conversational statistical analysis system that combines 417

agentic workflow orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and local R 418

execution. Using natural-language interaction, the system completed the prespecified 419

analytical workflow of a published study, including data-quality assessment, survival 420

analysis, Cox regression, model diagnostics, and generation of publication-formatted 421

tables and figures. Patient-level data processing and statistical computation remained 422

within the local workstation, while the external LLM was restricted to analytical 423

requirement refinement and R code generation using predefined dataset metadata and 424

retrieved statistical guidance. The principal contribution of this system is therefore not 425

simply automated code generation, but the architectural separation of external 426

LLM-assisted reasoning from local patient-level computation within an 427

investigator-supervised and auditable workflow. 428

Existing approaches to clinical data analysis often involve a trade-off between 431

analytical flexibility and ease of use. Programming environments such as R and 432

Python provide extensive flexibility and transparency but require proficiency in 433

statistical coding. In contrast, graphical and low-code platforms reduce programming 434

demands but generally require investigators to select appropriate methods, configure 435

analytical parameters, and interpret statistical assumptions. 436

Visual workflow platforms such as KNIME and Galaxy enable users to construct 437

low-code platforms such as LinkR further improve the accessibility of data 441

manipulation and statistical analysis. However, their functionality remains dependent 442

on the analytical modules and workflows implemented within the platform.7 443

Limitations and Future Directions 521

Several limitations of the current implementation warrant acknowledgment. The 522

non-deterministic nature of LLM code generation means that syntax errors or 523

suboptimal statistical choices may still occur. The current system captures execution 524

errors and terminates, but lacks an automated error-correction feedback loop, which is 525

an important direction for future development. Dependence on external LLM APIs 526

introduces vulnerability to network latency and service interruptions. The initial 527

construction and ongoing maintenance of the knowledge base require manual expert 528

curation; future work will explore semi-automated literature mining approaches to 529

reduce this burden. The system currently supports only structured tabular data and 530

does not yet extend to unstructured data types such as medical images or free-text 531

clinical notes. Furthermore, user input with high ambiguity or internal contradictions 532

may exceed the capacity of the current requirement clarification mechanism; a more 533
